problem: The claim that joining the two gives "more stiffness and strength per kilogram than either one" is false for the fibre. The chapter's own worked example proves it: the glass fibre alone has a specific modulus of 70 ÷ 2.5 = 28 GPa per g/cm³, while the composite is only 21.9. Along the fibre axis the composite is always weaker and less stiff per kilogram than the bare fibre; the real gain is over bulk metals and over the matrix alone.
fix: Joined, the pair gives far more stiffness and strength per kilogram than the matrix alone, and more than a metal part of the same weight — though never more than the bare fibre along its own axis.

problem: Aircraft brake discs are the standard example of carbon–carbon composites, not of SiC–SiC. Listing them under SiC–SiC teaches the wrong material for the wrong job.
fix: Turbine shrouds, heat shields and high-performance car brake discs. (Aircraft brakes are carbon–carbon, a different family.)

problem: A laminate is a way of stacking plies, not a fibre form like the other three bullets, and "stiff in two directions" is too narrow — plies can be laid at any angles, and a quasi-isotropic laminate is stiff in every in-plane direction.
fix: Move it out of the fibre list: Laminate: plies stacked at chosen angles, so the plate can be stiff in the directions you pick — a cross-ply laminate in two, a quasi-isotropic one in all in-plane directions.

problem: A cricket bat blade is willow. Carbon fibre appears only in the handle splice or toe guard of some bats, so listing "cricket bats" flatly under carbon fibre misleads.
fix: Aircraft panels, bicycle frames, and the handles and toe guards of some cricket bats (the blade itself is willow).

where: Quiz Q6 answer (and Section 2, heat limit)
problem: The 120–150 °C limit is an epoxy figure. Standard polyester matrices are usable only to roughly 60–100 °C, so the answer overstates polyester's heat resistance.
fix: Epoxy matrices soften or degrade near 120–150 °C and polyester well below that, so neither can survive 900 °C.

problem: The cross-reference to the resins chapter is typed as plain text "(5.6)" instead of a chapter link, so a student reading on a phone cannot tap through.
fix: Write it as a link to that chapter, e.g. "usually epoxy or polyester (5.6)".
